tier_reason: The README 'Decode speed' section gives first-party numbers against libopus 1.6.1 with compilers, flags and CPUs stated (GCC 15.1 MinGW-w64 -O3 -march=x86-64-v3, Apple clang 17; Core Ultra 9 185H, Apple M5), but the C program that links every decoder and produced the table is not published: tools/ holds only quality/ (Python metrics) and eval/ (an older Rust harness that times ffmpeg subprocesses), falcon_capi/examples holds roundtrip/decode examples, and no other pbtechlab repo or release asset carries it. Numbers exist, so C rather than D; no public harness, so not A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Falcon: workspace release profile (opt-level 3, lto = true i.e. fat LTO, codegen-units 1, panic abort), .cargo/config.toml target-cpu=x86-64-v3 on x86-64 targets, default aarch64 target on M5; on Windows the MSVC-toolchain DLL (a MinGW build decodes 1.45x slower, 771x). C decoders: -O3, GCC 15.1 (MinGW-w64) -march=x86-64-v3 on x86-64, Apple clang 17 default target on M5; libopus default SIMD (SSE4.1/AVX2 runtime dispatch, NEON on arm64), stack protector off. Each run times open + whole-file decode + close; at least 10 runs and 1 s per file; best run over two passes.
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers on one Intel laptop CPU and one Apple CPU; the C comparison harness that links all decoders is not in the repository (README: 'the cross-codec numbers ... come from a C harness that calls the C API'), so the table cannot be reproduced from public code; the 11 real recordings of the 18-file corpus are not redistributed (the 7 synthetic signals are regenerable with tools/quality/make_torture.py). Different work from the baseline: libopus decodes Opus bitstreams while Falcon decodes its own MDCT format, matched only on file size (Falcon encoded with --target-bytes at <= the Opus file size, 0.998-1.000x on 17 files and 0.53x on the sweep; Opus references are libopus VBR at 96-214 kbps with encoder settings not stated). Quality equivalence rests on Falcon's own metrics: lower MR-STFT on 18/18 and log-mel on 13/18, the perceptual A/B check 'same' overall, Opus better on 4 files (harpsichord, pinkbursts, polychord, sfxtransient), and the perceptual checker is not in the repo. Falcon lacks packet-loss concealment and a low-delay mode, which libopus provides. Raw libopus is fed pre-extracted packets (no Ogg parsing) while opusfile/vorbisfile/stb_vorbis include container parsing. Falcon uses about 318-345 KB heap per stereo stream plus a copy of the compressed file (libopus 27 KB), allocates about seven times per 20 ms frame, and its decoder-only code is 629 KB vs libopus 130 KB. stb_vorbis is 4% faster on the x86-64 P-core and 1.28x faster on M5. Earlier README versions compared against FFmpeg's built-in Opus/Vorbis decoders by mistake; the old Vorbis figures were withdrawn in v2.0.1 (against FFmpeg's Vorbis decoder Falcon wins only 5 of 18 files). Floating-point encoder/decoder agreement across platforms is untested. Very new project (2 stars).

notes: Numbers in claimed_speedup match the README table exactly (1114x vs libopus float 731x, 0.66x time; M5 1551x vs 1056x; 256 voices 291 ms vs 365 ms). No harness found anywhere public, so the record stays first-party C with the different-codec caveat stated; metadata (MIT, last commit 2026-09-29, not a fork) confirmed.

tier_reason: The harness is public (pytools/reporter.py driven by Makefile.toml and bench_runner/runner_scripts/run_all.sh) and report/system_info.md logs the CPU (GCP c2-standard-8, Xeon Cascade Lake) and rustc versions, but the C compiler version used for flac 1.4.3 is not logged and timing is one wall-clock run per file; more importantly no measured configuration does equal work: single-thread flacenc beats flac -8 only at a slightly worse ratio and loses to flac -5, and the multi-threaded win is 8 threads against single-threaded flac 1.4.3. First-party, short of A: C.

corrections.baseline: FLAC reference encoder: flac 1.4.3 command-line tool (-f -8, -f -8 --lax, -f -5), single-threaded (1.4.3 predates flac's -j threading)
corrections.claimed_speedup: Nightly report (simd-nightly): flacenc st 331.5x and mt1 353.1x real time vs flac -8 229.7x (st 1.44x faster, derived from page data) but vs flac -5 550.4x (st 0.60x, derived from page data); default with 8 worker threads 1309.5x (5.7x flac -8 and 2.38x flac -5, derived from page data) against single-threaded flac. Average compression rate (output/input, lower is better): flacenc 0.5276 vs flac -8 0.5256 (flacenc output about 0.4% larger, derived from page data) and flac -5 0.5328. Stable report (default build from crates.io without simd-nightly): st 126.5x, mt1 131.2x, default 575.3x vs flac -8 230.9x and -5 572.1x, so single-thread stable is 0.55x of flac -8 and the 8-thread default only matches flac -5 (derived from page data).
corrections.workload: Integration report from pytools/reporter.py: CLI against CLI (flacenc-bin vs the flac 1.4.3 binary), one wall-clock run (time.time around subprocess) per file and setting, including process start-up, WAV read and FLAC write; four Wikimedia recordings; reference settings opt8lax/opt8/opt5 and flacenc configs default (multithread, workers = logical cores = 8 on this VM), mt1 (multithread, 1 worker), st (single thread) and experimental (direct-MSE LPC); every flacenc output is decoded with flac -d and compared byte-for-byte with the input.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: flacenc-bin: rustc 1.95.0 stable and 1.97.0-nightly (2026-05-21) per report/system_info.md; release profile lto = fat, codegen-units 1, panic abort; .cargo/config.toml target-cpu=native; mimalloc, par, decode, experimental features; nightly report adds simd-nightly (portable_simd), stable report uses the fake portable_simd. flac 1.4.3 built with ./configure && make (configure.ac prepends -O3 -funroll-loops for GCC; no -march) inside a rust:1-slim-bookworm container with Debian build-essential; the C compiler version is not logged.
corrections.hardware: GCP c2-standard-8 VM (asia-northeast1-a): Intel Xeon @ 3.10GHz, family 6 model 85 stepping 7 (Cascade Lake, AVX-512), 4 cores / 8 threads, Debian 12, kernel 6.6.122 (report/system_info.md, 2026-05-22)
corrections.stars_or_usage: 41 stars, 11 forks; crates.io flacenc 0.5.1, about 703k downloads (177k recent)
corrections.caveats: No measured configuration is both faster and at equal-or-better compression than a tested flac setting: single-thread flacenc (st) beats flac -8 in speed (1.44x nightly) while producing about 0.4% larger files, and against flac -5, whose files are about 1% larger, it is slower (0.60x nightly). The headline multi-threaded default uses 8 worker threads (4 physical cores with SMT) against flac 1.4.3, which has no threading; flac 1.5.0 (February 2025) added multithreaded encoding (-j/--threads) and was not benchmarked. On stable Rust, the crates.io default build, flacenc st runs at 0.55x of flac -8 and the 8-thread default only ties flac -5. flacenc is built with target-cpu=native (AVX-512 on this VM) while flac uses its generic configure build. Timing is a single wall-clock run per file with process start-up and file I/O included, on four recordings, no repeats. CLI against CLI, not library against library. The benchmark machine changed in May 2026 (c2-standard-8 replaced e2-standard-8, PR #253). The README makes no explicit speed claim and only links the reports.

notes: Report numbers match the record; I added mt1, the derived ratios, and the compression-rate comparison the orchestrator asked for. Hardware, Rust versions and flags are now recorded from report/system_info.md and the bench_runner scripts. The flac 1.5 -j fact is from a WebSearch snippet (release-news results), not an opened page.

tier_reason: First-party README tables (AMD Ryzen 9 9950X) generated by tools/benchmark.py as it stood at cc9195a, which ran the ffmpeg CLI against the h26xdec example; that code is public in history, but the FFmpeg version and build, rustc version and flags are not stated, the Big Buck Bunny benchmark clips are not in the repo, and the current benchmark.py (6eb41d8) no longer runs FFmpeg, so the libavcodec rows cannot be regenerated: C.

corrections.workload: Decode of 720p Big Buck Bunny encodes (cabac3.264 and cavlc3.264, H.264 High from x264 CRF 20, 723 frames each; hevc6.265, H.265 Main from x265 without WPP, 1446 frames; wpp10.265, x265 with WPP, 1200 frames), clips repeated so a run lasts long enough for Windows' 15.6 ms CPU-time clock. Process-tree CPU seconds (Windows job object) and frames per wall second, best of 5. Single-thread rows pinned to one core for both decoders (ffmpeg -threads 1, H26X_THREADS=1); all-thread rows unpinned (ffmpeg with its default thread count, rivet with every core). libavcodec ran as 'ffmpeg -i clip -f rawvideo -y NUL' (rawvideo written to the null device); rivet ran examples/h26xdec with H26XDEC_NOMD5=1 (each picture packed and dropped).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for either decoder: the FFmpeg build was a scoop-installed ffmpeg of unstated version and configuration; rivet built with the default cargo release profile (no profile overrides in Cargo.toml), rustc version unstated. SIMD rung selected at run time (AVX-512 supplement on this CPU). The libavcodec rows came from tools/benchmark.py at commit cc9195a; the current tools/benchmark.py (since 6eb41d8, 2026-10-03) compares against the scalar rung only.
corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X 16-Core Processor, 32 hardware threads, Windows (job-object CPU accounting), AVX-512 rung; machine 17% busy before the run; single-thread rows pinned to core 29, all-thread rows unpinned
corrections.stars_or_usage: 0 stars, 0 forks; 515 commits; not on crates.io (crates.io API on 2026-10-04: crate 'rivet-h26x' does not exist) despite the README badge; moved from the rivet-transcoder organisation to safewords on 2026-10-03
corrections.caveats: Only one cell of four is ahead: all-threads on the wavefront H.265 clip wpp10.265 (1963 vs 1774 fps, +10.7%), and that cell is not equal work: rivet spent 4.656 CPU s against libavcodec's 2.656 (1.75x, per the README's own line) and used every hardware thread (32), while ffmpeg ran with libavcodec's automatic thread count, which libavcodec caps at min(logical CPUs + 1, 16) (MAX_AUTO_THREADS 16 in current FFmpeg master pthread_internal.h / pthread_frame.c; the FFmpeg version used is not stated), so most likely 16 threads on this machine. All-thread rows were unpinned on a machine 17% busy, with a byte-identical control spread of up to 4.0% in all-thread fps and a stated +-5% drift between sessions (wpp10.265 moved from 0.96x to 1.02x single-thread with no code change). Single-threaded, H.265 is at parity or slower (1.02x and 1.12x libavcodec's CPU time) and H.264 costs 1.46-1.55x; the H.264 all-thread gains (+2.4%, +1.7%) are inside the noise floor and the non-WPP H.265 clip is 7.1% slower. The comparison is ffmpeg CLI (demux plus rawvideo output to the null device) against the h26xdec example binary, not library against library. Output equivalence: both are normative decoders and rivet is bit-exact on the JVT and JCT-VC conformance suites and against JM/HM, so equal output is expected, but the benchmark itself did not compare outputs with libavcodec. The libavcodec rows are a 2026-09 record that the current tooling cannot regenerate, and the clips are not published. Open Encoding Attribution License v1.0 is source-available, not OSI (it says so itself: commercial attribution duty, field-of-use discrimination, not GPL-compatible), so usability is reference.

notes: README numbers match the record; I corrected the frame count of hevc6.265 (1446, not 1200) and the repo's new home (safewords). The key addition is the thread asymmetry on the one winning cell (rivet 32 threads and 1.75x CPU vs libavcodec's capped auto threads), found by reading the pre-6eb41d8 tools/benchmark.py and FFmpeg's thread code.
